groups.title: InnoDB & Storage Engine Internals
groups.question: Explain how InnoDB stores data and keeps it safe after a crash.

followUps.InnoDB Architecture — Buffer Pool & Redo: How do the buffer pool size and the redo log flush setting trade speed for safety?
followUps.Transaction Isolation Levels in MySQL: Why can range queries cause surprise deadlocks under REPEATABLE READ in InnoDB?

evidence.text: The buffer pool caches pages in memory; too small and queries hit disk.
The redo log records changes so committed work can be recovered after a crash.
Flushing the log on every commit is safest; flushing less often is faster but can lose recent commits on an OS crash or power loss.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (buffer pool, redo log) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the buffer pool is what makes data survive a crash.

evidence.text: MySQL's default isolation is REPEATABLE READ.
InnoDB locks the gaps between index records in range queries to prevent phantom rows.
Two transactions locking overlapping ranges can block each other and deadlock, even with simple-looking SQL.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (REPEATABLE READ, gap lock) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says InnoDB only ever locks the exact rows returned.

groups.title: MySQL vs PostgreSQL Differences
groups.question: Walk through the differences between MySQL and PostgreSQL that matter when you move between them.

followUps.Key Behavioral Differences: Why is it dangerous when a database accepts a bad value instead of raising an error?
followUps.Deadlocks & How to Detect Them: How does a deadlock happen, and what should the application do when InnoDB picks it as the victim?

evidence.text: With strict mode off, MySQL can silently truncate strings or store invalid dates instead of failing.
Bad data gets in without anyone noticing and is found much later.
An error at write time makes the bug visible immediately, which PostgreSQL and strict mode do.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (strict mode, truncation) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says silently truncating values is harmless.

evidence.text: A deadlock is two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds.
InnoDB detects it and rolls back one of them.
The application must catch that error and retry the transaction, and keep a consistent lock order to make it rarer.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (deadlock, lock) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a deadlock leaves both transactions waiting forever.

groups.title: MySQL Configuration & Tuning
groups.question: Explain how you would tune a MySQL server and find the queries that slow it down.

followUps.my.cnf — Key Configuration Variables: Which configuration settings would you check first on a new production MySQL server, and why?
followUps.Slow Query Log & Performance Schema: How would you use the slow query log and Performance Schema without slowing production down?

evidence.text: The defaults are sized for a tiny machine.
innodb_buffer_pool_size should be raised to fit the working set in memory.
Other first checks: max_connections and redo log size.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (my.cnf, innodb_buffer_pool_size) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says production can run on default settings.

evidence.text: The slow query log records queries slower than a threshold, showing which to fix first.
Performance Schema gives detailed timings for waits and statements.
Enable only the instruments you need, because turning everything on adds overhead.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (slow query log, Performance Schema) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says you should log every query at full detail in production.

groups.title: Stored Procedures & Events
groups.question: Walk through when it makes sense to run logic or scheduled jobs inside MySQL itself.

followUps.MySQL Stored Procedures: What problems appear when important business logic lives in stored procedures?
followUps.MySQL Event Scheduler: What happens when a scheduled event fails, and how would you make sure someone notices?

evidence.text: Logic in procedures lives outside the app's code and often outside version control.
They are hard to test and debug.
They drift from the application and become a hidden second codebase.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (stored procedure) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says business logic should always live in stored procedures for speed.

evidence.text: A failed scheduled event has no retry and no visible log by default, so it fails silently.
You make it noticeable by logging errors, writing a status row, or alerting when the job didn't run.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (event scheduler) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the event scheduler retries failed events.
